extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism history; readers interested in late-19th-century American newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Historical analysis of the rise of the 'New Journalism' and the organizational, editorial, and commercial practices that made newspapers successful in the United States between 1872 and 1892.

rubrics_metrics.name: News policy
rubrics_metrics.description: A staff of alert and persistent reporters scoured the city for incidents, events, and situations which could be made interesting; these were presented as colorfully as possible, and given heads which were unusual and often sensational. Use of the telegraph and cable news (even for gossip and trivial news) was an element of this policy, though important and significant news remained the backbone of the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize energetic, persistent local reporting; combine serious world news coverage with lighter, exciting items to enliven the paper. Use bold, unusual headlines and exploit telegraphic speed—but balance sensational items so they do not displace important reporting. (The World tended to tone down sensationalism after 1887.)

rubrics_metrics.name: World crusades and 'stunts'
rubrics_metrics.description: Crusades and 'stunts'—organized campaigns and high-publicity enterprises—were central: e.g., fundraising for the Statue of Liberty pedestal, Nellie Bly's voyage around the world, undercover exposes (feigning insanity to enter an asylum), polls and censuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use crusades and stunts to mobilize public interest and effect reform; combine human-interest spectacle with investigative reporting. Examples show they can raise funds, change policy, and build readership; but stunts must be planned to attract and sustain public engagement (contests, daily buildup, prizes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial page of high character
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial page regarded as the heart of the paper and the chief reason for its existence; used to bring crusades to a head and to serve as a leading spokesman on public issues (e.g., liberal ideas, antimonopoly stance, support for income/inheritance taxes, siding with unions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate strong, principled editorials that synthesize reporting crusades into coherent public positions. Editorials amplify the paper's political influence but may also attract controversy; they should be intellectually sustained and central to the paper's identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size (page count and low price)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing the number of pages while keeping a low price (e.g., two-cent or one-cent papers expanding from eight to fourteen or sixteen pages) was a factor in success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer more content per issue at competitive prices to attract mass readership; larger issues permit more news items, advertising space, and variety (features, sports, illustrations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration and cartoons
rubrics_metrics.description: Leadership in newspaper illustration—single-column portraits, cuts of events (bridges, fires), diagrams of crime scenes, and political cartoons—enhanced the paper's appeal (e.g., Walt McDougall, Valerian Gribayedoff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate illustrations and cartoons to make stories vivid and to draw readers' attention; develop regular cartoon features and increase picture usage over time (color printing and banner heads would be added later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion (coupons, contests, self-praise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active promotion—coupons, voting contests, boastful self-praise—was an important part of circulation-building, even when it offended some sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contests and promotional devices as effective advertising to the average reader; balance promotional techniques with editorial credibility to avoid reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulitzer's newspaper-writing creed
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer summed up needed qualities as: 'terseness, humor, descriptive power, satire, originality, good literary style, clever condensation, and accuracy, accuracy, accuracy!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize concise, vivid, and stylistically strong prose combined with rigorous accuracy; treat accuracy as nonnegotiable and repeatedly emphasized in editorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism (definition, use, and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensationalism defined broadly as subject matter and treatment that excite emotions—detailed treatment of crimes, disasters, sex scandals, and monstrosities. The New Journalism emphasized sensational items to attract readers, though sensationalism had antecedents and should not wholly replace substantial news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize sensational material as an attention-getting tool that can enliven a paper, but be aware of moral criticism and the need to retain accuracy and substantive reporting. Once circulation is established, accuracy and truth are essential for lasting success (Julius Chambers' observation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Undercover 'stunt' reporting and exposés
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactics included disguise, feigning insanity, forging documents, or otherwise infiltrating institutions (hospitals, jails, asylums) to produce exposés and narratives of experience that reveal administrative abuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such methods can produce powerful investigative stories and social reform but raise ethical issues (privacy, deception); they were widely used in the period and often allied with crusading aims (Nellie Bly's asylum expose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invasion of privacy / 'keyhole journalism' (critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic practices that pry into private lives—gossip and scandal columns dragging innocent persons into copy—were condemned as indecent and labeled 'keyhole journalism.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of gossip-driven reporting that invades privacy; such practice invites moral and legal criticism (e.g., the Right to Privacy debate by Warren and Brandeis) and can damage public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing (question-and-answer technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal Q&A interviewing was criticized when questions were flippant and replies ill-considered; critics said 'interviewing makes fools of great men,' though practitioners argued it is valuable if used seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviewing responsibly: avoid frivolous or sensational questioning; employ interviews as a serious tool to elicit meaningful information and human detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports and local news specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Expansion of sports coverage (turf men, baseball reporters) and dedicated sporting editors; increased local news led to promotion of the city editor and development of news bureaus/agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialize reporting beats (sports, local) and create dedicated editorial structures (sporting editors, city editors, bureaus) to provide comprehensive coverage and attract readers with diverse interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staff organization and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Growing staffs (forty or fifty reporters, multiple desk editors) and complex organization changed journalism from highly personal editors to institutional operations; city editors became second only to managing editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design editorial hierarchy and desk organization to manage larger newsgathering operations while preserving quality and editorial direction; acknowledge tradeoffs between scale and personal-authority editorialism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evening-paper publication strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods included 'late editions' of morning papers, separate evening papers (or editions) timed to capture different crowds; evening papers often issued three to five editions and targeted street sales, home-bound workers, theatre crowds, and women readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit telegraphic speed and multiple daily editions to refresh content and reach distinct readerships; position evening issues to attract advertisers (department stores) and maximize street and home delivery sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circulation–advertising–profit linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising volume followed circulation—papers that grew circulation often saw advertising increase (e.g., the World passed the Herald in ad volume), leading to record profitability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue circulation growth strategies (price, promotion, content breadth) to attract advertisers; balance editorial choices that build readership with commercial imperatives that sustain profitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crusading/reform journalism as public service
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers conducted campaigns against monopolies, corrupt politicians, lotteries, and social abuses and provided public services (free ice/coal, medical staffs, excursions, festivals) as part of civic engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame investigative and crusading efforts to effect concrete reforms and public benefit; combine reporting with organized charitable or civic actions to demonstrate public-mindedness and reinforce the paper's role as 'the people's paper.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and truth as foundation of enduring success
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary observers asserted that while sensationalism helps build an audience, 'absolute accuracy and truth are the only bases for enduring success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat accuracy and factual truth as the long-term basis of credibility and sustainability; sensational devices should not undercut factual rigor.
